source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module B unit 2: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Analyse hidden alteration and the separate sender/receiver duties for truncated cheque images

facts.statement: Section 89(1) protects the specified payer when a material alteration is not apparent and payment follows apparent tenor and is otherwise in due course. Subsections (2)–(3) impose image/original exactness on truncation/transmission and verification of image sameness with the transmitting party on receipt. Section 131 Explanation II requires the collecting banker's ordinary-care check of apparent genuineness of the cheque held for truncation.
facts.locator: S04 printed pp. 158–159, 161; PDF page = printed page + 19

payload.title: Hidden alteration does not remove the due-course conditions
payload.core_explanation_md:
Section 89 addresses an alteration that does **not appear on presentation**, including the specified crossing situations. Its protection requires payment according to the apparent terms and otherwise in due course. The section does not excuse ignoring an alteration that is visible or other circumstances that defeat the due-course test.

Separate the questions in a disputed payment: what change was made, whether it was apparent at payment, what ordinary checks were performed and whether the rest of the payment met the required conditions. Later forensic discovery of a change does not by itself answer all of them.

self_check.prompt_text: Does discovering an alteration later prove that Section 89 protection was unavailable?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Apparency at payment and the remaining statutory conditions must be examined.

payload.title: Check both links in the cheque-image chain
payload.core_explanation_md:
Truncation creates more than one integrity task. Under Section 89(2), the bank or clearing house must ensure the image's apparent terms match the paper cheque when truncating and transmitting it. Under Section 89(3), a receiving bank or clearing house verifies with the transmitting party that the image received is exactly the image sent.

These checks answer different questions. A perfectly transmitted image can still misrepresent the paper cheque. Separately, Section 131 Explanation II requires the collecting banker holding the cheque for truncation to check its apparent genuineness with ordinary care. Passing a transmission check does not replace that original-instrument check.

self_check.prompt_text: Can proof that received and transmitted images match establish that the image matches the paper original?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Image-to-image transmission integrity and image-to-original exactness are different checks.

payload.stem_md: A bank confirms that its received cheque image is identical to the sender's transmitted image. The image nevertheless shows an amount different from the paper original. Which failure remains possible?

options.text_md: No failure is possible once the network transmission is accurate
options.explanation_md: Transmission accuracy does not prove that the image accurately represents the paper cheque.

options.text_md: Failure to ensure image-to-original exactness at truncation or transmission
options.explanation_md: Section 89(2) addresses this distinct link; Section 89(3) verification alone does not establish it.

options.text_md: Automatic conversion of the cheque into a bearer note
options.explanation_md: An image mismatch concerns integrity and possible alteration, not conversion to a different instrument type.

options.text_md: Failure by the payee to become the cheque's drawer
options.explanation_md: A payee need not become the drawer, and this does not address the mismatch.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Section 89(2) addresses this distinct link; Section 89(3) verification alone does not establish it.

payload.stem_md: A visible unauthenticated change to a cheque amount is ignored at payment. A manager later invokes Section 89 solely because the change was fraudulent. What is the central flaw?

options.text_md: Section 89 applies only where no fraud could ever exist
options.explanation_md: The section can address concealed alteration; fraud in itself is not the disqualifying feature described here.

options.text_md: Every amount alteration is automatically accepted by the drawer
options.explanation_md: Consent or authority cannot be assumed merely because an amount has been changed.

options.text_md: Any later discovery makes all earlier checks irrelevant
options.explanation_md: What was apparent at payment and the checks made remain central to the analysis.

options.text_md: The change was apparent and ignored; concealment and due-course conditions cannot simply be assumed
options.explanation_md: Section 89 does not supply blanket protection for a visible defect or negligent payment.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Section 89 does not supply blanket protection for a visible defect or negligent payment.

payload.stem_md: A bank holds the paper cheque for truncation. It proposes to verify only that the image file opens successfully and omit ordinary-care checks for apparent tampering on the paper. Which response best identifies the missing duty?

options.text_md: Image usability does not replace the collecting banker's apparent-genuineness check
options.explanation_md: Section 131 Explanation II separately addresses ordinary-care checks of the cheque held for truncation.

options.text_md: A readable image conclusively proves a genuine drawer signature
options.explanation_md: File readability supplies no conclusive proof of signature genuineness.

options.text_md: The receiving bank alone bears every duty in truncation
options.explanation_md: The statutory duties also concern the truncating and transmitting parties and the collecting banker holding the cheque.

options.text_md: Paper checks are prohibited once imaging equipment is installed
options.explanation_md: Truncation starts from paper; imaging does not prohibit the required examination of that paper.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Section 131 Explanation II separately addresses ordinary-care checks of the cheque held for truncation.
